newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Wheat hits 6-month high, oil steady, gold falls.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Wheat hits 6-month high, oil steady, gold falls.

text.p: Wheat prices soared on Friday as unseasonably cold, wintry weather kept an icy grip on young wheat plants in the United States.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for May delivery closed 10 cents a bushel higher at $4.03, its highest closing price since September 27, 1996.

Traders said this week's blast of freezing cold and snows from the Dakotas to Texas had grown into a threat to winter wheat planted last fall and now struggling to emerge on schedule with spring. The crop is harvested in June and July.

The latest bad weather comes on the heels of heavy snowfalls this winter in the Dakotas and Minnesota, where spring wheat is usually planted. Flooding due to the snowmelt could push back planting or mean less acreage is seeded.

"We do have dynamics changing quite a bit for wheat," said Bob Lekberg, analyst for Chicago-based trade house Goldenberg Hehmeyer. "There's a potential disruption in plantings in the northern U.S. spring wheat area and cold weather is coming into the winter (wheat) area."

Much of the winter wheat in the High Plains states that produce about half the U.S. wheat crop is in the jointing stage, in which the seed-producing head of the plant starts moving up the stalk and creating leaves, or tillers.
A severe freeze could kill the tillers, and Saturday morning's low temperatures were expected to dip below freezing as far south as the Texas panhandle.
"What likely will happen is the tillers jointing now will be killed," said Gary Paulsen, an agronomy professor at Kansas State University in Manhattan, Kansas.
Traders also cited potential dry-weather stress to the European wheat crop as central to Friday's gains, as no significant rains for young winter wheat there are forecast.
Earlier this week, the French government ordered farmers in the Beauce, Europe's biggest grain-producing region, to reduce irrigation of crops due to early signs of drought.
The threats to this year's crop come as wheat stocks continue near the lowest levels in two decades.
The Agriculture Department on Friday cut its estimate for wheat stocks in the United States at the end of the current season on May 31 to 460 million bushels from 474 million.
Soybean stocks were also cut to a projected 125 million bushels on September 1 this year, down from 140 million last month and the lowest level in 20 years.

However, soybean traders focused instead on a weekly report released late on Thursday showing a sharp drop in weekly soybean crushing to 25.94 million bushels, the lowest pace of demand from soybean processors since October.

That signal of a let-up in red-hot commercial demand sparked heavy selling. Soybeans for May delivery closed 24-3/4 cents a bushel lower at $8.30-1/2 and down nearly 37 cents from the morning's highest traded price.
Corn stockpiles were also estimated lower but the huge sell-off in soybeans pushed corn prices to a lower close, with May delivery corn ending at $2.99-1/2, down 4-1/4 cents.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices ended slightly lower as an early boost from diplomatic tensions between European Union countries and Iran faded.
On Thursday, a German court implicated Iran's leaders in the killing of four Kurdish dissidents at a Berlin restaurant.
Following the verdict, many European countries recalled their ambassadors for consultations. Iran ordered four German diplomats home and recalled its ambassador in Bonn.
But European oil companies including France's Total and Anglo-Dutch oil giant Shell said their operations in Iran would not be affected by the diplomatic tensions.

"I think the feeling is that if it were that serious the EU would impose sanctions, but they haven't. In any case, a situation like that would affect Brent (North Sea oil) more, and Brent failed to hold gains too," said Michael Busby, trader with Northville Industries in Melville, New York.
"The news does not change the fact that there is still plenty of crude supply in the Atlantic basin," said Busby.

Crude for May delivery settled four cents a barrel lower at $19.53 on the New York Mercantile Exchange. May gasoline ended off 0.19 cent a gallon at 60.88 cents while May heating oil ended off 0.99 cent at 53.87 cents a gallon.
Precious metals closed lower as commodity fund investors sold when economic data raised fears of higher interest rates.
June gold at the COMEX in New York ended at $349.30 an ounce, down $1.60, while May silver ended at $4.72 an ounce, down 6.2 cents.
In Friday's data, the March Producer Price Index fell 0.1 percent but its core rate excluding food and energy rose a higher-than-expected 0.4 percent.

"With the market and the Fed driving real interest rates higher, precious metals look less attractive, while the weakness in the stock market is not yet pronounced enough to encourage a move into gold," Chase Manhattan New York managing director Dinsa Mehta said.
